title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
The Hanover Institute case shows a deliberate attempt to exploit a known property of AI systems: that large language models and AI chatbots draw on indexed web content when generating citations and summaries. The institute published a high volume of documents in a short period using a platform specifically configured to make that content attractive to AI retrieval systems. The failure this exposes is not in the AI models themselves but in the conditions under which they surface sources, namely that volume, formatting, and technical optimization can substitute for legitimacy, making fabricated institutional authority difficult to distinguish from genuine scholarship.

The operation was caught through investigative reporting, not through any AI platform's own detection. Nothing in the summary indicates that the chatbot systems being targeted had any mechanism to verify whether a cited organization legally exists, employs named researchers, or represents disclosed interests. The gap exploited here sits at the retrieval and citation layer of deployed AI systems, before any human review would typically occur.

What is not established is whether any AI system actually cited the Hanover Institute's content in responses to users, or whether the campaign achieved its intended effect on public opinion or policy.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

A fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute, funded by the Israeli government, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in just nine days. The institute does not legally exist in any jurisdiction and has no named staff. The reports were designed to appear as neutral academic research while presenting pro-Israel positions on controversial topics including alleged war crimes, torture of Palestinian prisoners, and whether Israel caused starvation in Gaza. The site used a platform optimized to make artificial intelligence chatbots cite its content, representing part of a broader multimillion-dollar campaign involving Israeli government agencies, European advertising firm Havas Media, and American contractors.

The campaign cost tens of millions of dollars, with Israeli firm Havas paying approximately $24.9 million to American contractors between late 2025 and early 2026. The Hanover Institute was registered with the U.S. Justice Department as Israeli government material under foreign agent disclosure laws. Israeli officials privately expressed doubt about the campaign's effectiveness, with one stating the government paid considerable money but the situation only worsened. American public opinion has increasingly favored Palestinians, with support for Israel declining significantly since 2022.
